note: S120b — enhancement (b) `dilationExplore.showRatios` reached 2 lessons of the ~8 the playbook named. These three are the ones whose authored prose already describes the drag; the rest of the sy- residue is recorded in PLAYBOOK_STATUS.md as needing engine work the enhancement does not have.

widget.prompt: The small triangle has the two sides 4 and 6 meeting at a right angle. Drag k until the image is the triangle with 6 and 9 — and watch whether the angle between them ever moves.
widget.successFeedback: k = 1.5: the 4 became 6 and the 6 became 9, both by the same factor, and the readout confirms every length went up by 1.5. The included angle never budged — a dilation cannot change an angle. Two sides in a common ratio plus that fixed angle between them is exactly what SAS~ asks for.
widget.lowFeedback: The image is still too small — 4 has not reached 6 yet. Keep opening k, and notice that both sides are growing together rather than one at a time.
widget.highFeedback: Past it: the image has overshot 6 and 9. Ease k back down. Whatever you do to k happens to both sides at once, which is why a single number can describe the whole pair.

predict.prompt: Two triangles have sides 4 and 6, and 6 and 9, with equal included angles. Dilating the first onto the second will need…

options.label: One scale factor that works for both sides
A different scale factor for each side
No single dilation — the angle would change too

predict.reveal: One factor, 1.5, and it moves both sides together — that is what makes the ratio 'common'. And the angle is untouched, because a dilation stretches distances and leaves directions alone.

widget.prompt: The preimage is the 3-4-5 triangle. Drag k until the image is the 9-12-15 triangle, and check all three sides as you go — not just the one you are watching.
widget.successFeedback: k = 3, and 3-4-5 has become 9-12-15 — every side tripled, which the perimeter readout reports as one number. That is SSS~: not three separate coincidences but a single dilation, so the triangles are similar and the scale factor is 3.
widget.lowFeedback: Not yet — the image is still short of 9-12-15. Keep raising k, and watch all three sides climb in step rather than one catching up to the others.
widget.highFeedback: Too far: the image has passed 9-12-15. Bring k down. No value of k stretches one side without stretching the other two by the same amount, which is the whole point.

predict.prompt: Triangle A is 3-4-5, triangle B is 9-12-15. Checking SSS~ means checking…

options.label: All three ratios, and finding they are equal
One ratio — the others must follow
The angles, since sides cannot settle similarity

predict.reveal: All three — the criterion is that they agree, and agreement is the thing being tested. What the dilation shows is why they agree when they do: one factor is acting on every side at once.

widget.prompt: The arrows mark the inner segment as parallel to the base — that is what the marks are telling you. Slide the cut to the midpoint of AB and read both ratios the whole way.
widget.successFeedback: Both ratios read 1.00 — the cut has bisected AB and AC at once. The marks are the whole warrant: because the segment is parallel to the base, the two ratios are locked together, so cutting one side in half cuts the other in half too. That is the side-splitter theorem, and the midpoint case is the midsegment.
widget.lowFeedback: The cut is still above the midpoint — AD/DB is under 1.00. Keep sliding down, and watch the second ratio track the first the entire way rather than lagging behind it.
widget.highFeedback: Past the midpoint now — AD/DB has gone above 1.00. Ease back up. Notice that overshooting moved both readouts together; they have never once disagreed.

predict.prompt: A segment inside a triangle is marked parallel to the base. Sliding it up and down, the two side ratios AD/DB and AE/EC will…

options.label: Always match each other, at every position
Move independently — they measure different sides

predict.reveal: Always. Parallel to the base is the condition, and it holds at every height, so the two ratios are equal everywhere the cut can go. The midpoint is not where the theorem starts working — it is just the position where both ratios happen to read 1.
